nodes.name: Near, not at
nodes.statement: A limit describes the values of f(x) as x gets close to a point a. It says nothing about the value at a itself.

nodes.name: Informal limit
nodes.statement: lim (x→a) f(x) = L means f(x) can be made as close to L as desired by taking x close enough to a, with x ≠ a.

nodes.name: f(a) does not matter
nodes.statement: The limit at a ignores f(a) completely. It can exist even when f(a) is undefined or different from L.

nodes.name: Removable hole
nodes.statement: f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) is undefined at x = 1 but equals x + 1 for every other x. So its limit at 1 is 2.

nodes.name: Tolerance ε
nodes.statement: In the formal definition, a number ε > 0 states how close f(x) must be to L, the demand |f(x) − L| < ε.

nodes.name: Closeness δ
nodes.statement: In the formal definition, a number δ > 0 states how close x must be to a, the condition 0 < |x − a| < δ.

nodes.name: ε-δ definition
nodes.statement: lim (x→a) f(x) = L means that for every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 such that 0 < |x − a| < δ implies |f(x) − L| < ε.

nodes.name: Challenge and response
nodes.statement: The definition works like a game. A challenger names any tolerance ε, and the limit holds if a matching δ can always be found.

nodes.name: δ depends on ε
nodes.statement: The δ may depend on the ε that was demanded. Smaller tolerances usually require smaller δ.

nodes.name: Proof for 3x + 1
nodes.statement: For f(x) = 3x + 1 at a = 2, choosing δ = ε/3 gives |f(x) − 7| = 3|x − 2| < ε. So lim (x→2) (3x + 1) = 7.

nodes.name: Limits are unique
nodes.statement: A function cannot approach two different numbers L and M at the same point. With ε = |L − M|/2, f(x) would have to be close to both at once, which is impossible.

nodes.name: One-sided limits
nodes.statement: A one-sided limit considers x on only one side of a. It is written x→a⁺ for x > a and x→a⁻ for x < a.

nodes.name: Two sides must agree
nodes.statement: The two-sided limit exists and equals L if and only if both one-sided limits exist and equal L.

nodes.name: A jump has no limit
nodes.statement: The sign function approaches −1 from the left of 0 and 1 from the right. So it has no limit at 0.

nodes.name: Oscillation has no limit
nodes.statement: sin(1/x) takes every value between −1 and 1 on every interval around 0. No single L can keep it within ε = 1/2, so it has no limit at 0.

nodes.name: Limit laws
nodes.statement: If f(x) → L and g(x) → M as x → a, then f + g → L + M and f·g → L·M. Also f/g → L/M, provided M ≠ 0.

nodes.name: Continuity at a point
nodes.statement: A function f is continuous at a when f(a) is defined and lim (x→a) f(x) = f(a).

nodes.name: Polynomials are continuous
nodes.statement: Constants and x itself have obvious limits, and the limit laws combine them. So every polynomial is continuous everywhere.

nodes.name: Direct substitution
nodes.statement: For a function continuous at a, the limit at a is found by plugging in a.

nodes.name: 0/0 is indeterminate
nodes.statement: When substitution gives 0/0, the quotient law does not apply and the form says nothing about the limit. The limit must be found another way, such as by cancelling a common factor.

nodes.name: Squeeze theorem
nodes.statement: If g(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ h(x) near a, and g and h both approach L, then f also approaches L.

nodes.name: sin(x)/x → 1
nodes.statement: For 0 < |x| < π/2, cos x ≤ (sin x)/x ≤ 1. Since cos x → 1, the squeeze theorem gives lim (x→0) (sin x)/x = 1.

nodes.name: x·sin(1/x) → 0
nodes.statement: Since −|x| ≤ x·sin(1/x) ≤ |x| and both bounds approach 0, x·sin(1/x) approaches 0 as x → 0. Multiplying by x tames the oscillation.

nodes.name: Derivative as a limit
nodes.statement: The derivative f′(a) is the limit of the slope (f(a + h) − f(a))/h as h → 0.

nodes.name: Every derivative is 0/0
nodes.statement: Plugging h = 0 into the difference quotient always gives 0/0. So no derivative can be computed by direct substitution, and every derivative needs a limit.

nodes.name: Limits at infinity
nodes.statement: lim (x→∞) f(x) = L means that for every ε > 0 there is a number N such that x > N implies |f(x) − L| < ε.

nodes.name: 1/x → 0
nodes.statement: For any ε > 0, choosing N = 1/ε gives |1/x| < ε for all x > N. So 1/x approaches 0 as x → ∞.
